text:
Abraham is commanded to take his son, his only son, whom he loves; and of what he feels at the command we are told nothing. The narrator will not look into him. There is no protest, no bargaining, nothing of the man who pleaded with God for Sodom, and who brought the number of the righteous down from fifty to ten. In this place he is scarcely a character at all; he is a silence, and in that silence, I think, lies the whole meaning of the episode. A question is put to us at the outset which is never answered.

The three days of the journey may be read as a kind of suspended sentence. Outwardly nothing happens; inwardly everything happens. The narrator dwells upon the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire, and so names the instruments of the act before he comes to the act itself. Obedience and horror are kept equally before us, and the writer suffers neither to prevail over the other. Faith, as it is here exhibited, is no feeling in the breast; it is rather a geometry, a fixed relation of lines that nothing in the mind of Abraham is permitted to disturb.

If we place the scene beside the earlier promise, the distance between promise and test grows less. Isaac is the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; and it is this very promise that the chapter converts into a trial. The whole scene turns upon a single word, 'hineni,' 'here I am,' which Abraham speaks three times: once to God, once to Isaac, once to the angel. Each time the word bears a different meaning; each time it costs him more. To declare himself present is, for Abraham, to declare himself ready to lose.

What does Isaac know? We are not told. He carries the wood; he asks where the lamb is; he receives an answer that is no answer. Of his thoughts the narrator gives us nothing, only a verb: they went, both of them, together. The phrase recurs, and the repetition seems to stand in the place of explanation. The question of Isaac's consent is raised and then quietly laid aside. Obedience, if we reckon it strictly, leaves nothing over and nothing unaccounted for.

The reader who attends to what is missing will be rewarded. Sarah has no part in the chapter; and in the verse that immediately follows it her death is announced. We are led to suspect, though it is nowhere said, that something in the household of Abraham did not come down from the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants; of Isaac there is no mention. At the very moment when a lesser writer would have lingered, the narrator turns away. Much of the meaning of the passage lies in what it omits, and its silences are full where they seem empty.

It may be objected that this reticence is merely the habit of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains. In some sense the objection may be true. Yet the same narrator elsewhere tells us plainly what his people feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is therefore deliberate; the writer chose it, and did not fall into it by custom. In his hands restraint becomes a kind of accusation.

The opposition between the God who promises and the God who demands is never resolved; the narrator keeps both before us and will not choose. Abraham stands upon the mountain with the knife raised, and the ram is not yet seen; and the reader is left where Abraham is left. The question cannot be answered, and its want of an answer is the only answer we receive. To read the chapter is to undergo a trial of one's own.

Genesis 22, in the end, is less a story of sacrifice than a story of reading; from it we learn that the things of most consequence are the things a writer declines to say. Abraham is silent; Isaac asks his question; Sarah is absent; the narrator refuses to explain. Each of these is a gap in the narrative, and each gap lays a demand upon us. The brevity of the chapter becomes the burden of its reader, and what is withheld from us is what we are given. We are left, at the last, with the knife, the wood, and the two of them going on together.
